newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's LVMH says it has deal to buy duty-free chain DFS.
newsitem.headline: France's LVMH says it has deal to buy duty-free chain DFS.

text.p: French luxury goods flagship LVMH said Wednesday it had an agreement to buy 59 percent of DFS, a privately held chain of duty-free shops based in San Francisco, for 12.6 billion french francs ($2.5 billion).

The announced deal, however, was thrown into doubt by reports that a major owner of DFS, the world's largest distributor of luxury goods, was resisting the sale to LVMH, whose products include Moet & Chandon champagnes, Hennessy cognacs, Christian Dior perfumes and Louis Vuitton luggage.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that billionaire investor Robert Miller, who owns 38.75 percent of DFS, opposed the sale and was seeking in court to have it blocked.
LVMH acknowledged that its acquisition of the 58.75 percent of DFS owned by co-founder Charles Feeney and company tax lawyer Alan Parker hinged on certain conditions, but did not elaborate.
"We can't say any more until the deal is finalised," a spokeswoman said. Industry sources in France said LVMH was waiting for a resolution of the dispute among DFS' owners.

The New York Times reported that Miller was insisting that the deal would violate the terms of an agreement the partners signed in 1991 to refer disputes to an independent arbitrator, long-time company lawyer Ira Millstein.

The newspaper quoted a representative as saying that Miller and company accountant Anthony Pilaro, who owns 2 percent of DFS, had offered to buy out Feeney and Parker for the same price LVMH was offering, but they were rebuffed.

The representative, Hartley Rogers, a managing director at investment bank Morgan Stanley, was quoted as saying that Miller and Pilaro did not want DFS controlled by LVMH, the company's biggest supplier and a major competitor.
None of the principals involved could be reached early Wednesday to comment.

The deal, which would boost LVMH's presence around the affluent Pacific Rim, would mark an unusual foray for Louis Vuitton Moet Hennessy into the retail industry, expanding its activities from production of designer goods to marketing and sales.
"Thanks to this acquisition, LVMH will increase its presence in the Asia-Pacific region and emerging countries, a future growth area," it said in a statement.
DFS, which has 20 years of experience in retailing in Asia, had annual sales of almost $3 billion last year.
"This deal has fabulous development potential for us. It's a diversification that's linked directly to our business," the LVMH spokeswoman told Reuters.
LVMH generated more than half its sales of 29.8 billion francs ($5.8 billion) last year in the United States and the Far East.
Shares in LVMH, one of the bluest chips on the Paris bourse, gained about 3.9 percent on the news.
"It's a very good deal," one trader said. But he added that the market had few details.
LVMH said in its statement that it would keep DFS' management team in place and that the chain would be managed independently of LVMH's other businesses.
However, the New York Times said that under the agreement, LVMH would have the right to change or even terminate the contracts of "15 to 20" key employees.
